config.title: Pagination

intro.title: Pagination
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React application that displays a list of items with pagination controls. You will learn how to manage and display data in separate pages, allowing users to navigate through large datasets easily. The core programming concept involves using React state hooks to track the current page and calculate which items to show. You'll work with TypeScript to define types for your data and props, and use basic JSX to render the list and navigation buttons.
intro.usecase: Pagination is essential for managing large datasets in real-world applications like e-commerce product listings, search engine results, and social media feeds. Developers implement pagination in dashboards displaying analytics data, admin panels showing user records, and content management systems with article lists. This pattern prevents performance issues by loading data in manageable chunks while providing intuitive navigation controls. Every time you click 'Next' on Google search results or browse through pages of products on Amazon, you're interacting with pagination implemented by developers.

objectives: Define a TypeScript interface to represent pagination state with properties for current page, items per page, and total items.
Implement React state hooks to store and update pagination data within a component.
Apply arithmetic operations to calculate the total number of pages based on total items and items per page.
Use array methods to slice data arrays and display only the items for the current page.
Construct reusable UI components to display pagination controls with page numbers.
Handle click events on pagination buttons to update the current page state.
Execute conditional rendering to disable navigation buttons when on the first or last page.
Utilize useEffect hooks to fetch or update data when the current page changes.
Control component behavior by implementing logic to prevent invalid page numbers.
Return structured JSX that combines data display with interactive pagination controls.
Access and display page metadata (e.g., 'Page X of Y') using computed pagination values.
Modify pagination parameters (items per page) and observe how the UI and calculations update.

steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement for React and useState is added to the file.
successCriteria: The code includes an import statement that imports React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import statement needs to include both React and useState from 'react'. Make sure you're importing them correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import both React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the main Pagination component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Pagination that returns JSX.Element. Define it after the imports.
steps.hint: Use either a function declaration or arrow function. Make sure it returns JSX.Element type.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the Pagination component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named Pagination is defined and returns JSX.Element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the Pagination component. This is the foundation for our pagination implementation.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've created a component named 'Pagination' that returns JSX.Element. Check your syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. You need to define a functional component named Pagination that returns JSX.Element.

steps.title: Initialize currentPage state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside your Pagination component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'currentPage' and its setter function 'setCurrentPage', initialized to 1.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to specify the type as number since page numbers are numeric.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a numeric state variable
const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable 'currentPage' initialized to 1, ready to track the current page number.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the currentPage state with useState. The component now has state to track which page is currently active.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've: 1) named the variable 'currentPage' and setter 'setCurrentPage', 2) initialized it to 1, and 3) used proper TypeScript typing for numbers.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Inside the component, use useState<number>(1) to create currentPage and setCurrentPage. Make sure you're using the useState hook correctly with TypeScript.

steps.title: Initialize totalPages state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside the Pagination component, add a second useState hook to create a state variable called 'totalPages' and its setter function 'setTotalPages'. Initialize it with the value 10.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook from React. The syntax is similar to the currentPage state you already created.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a second state variable
const [totalPages, setTotalPages] = useState<number>(10);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have two state variables: currentPage and totalPages, both initialized with numbers.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call that declares 'totalPages' and 'setTotalPages', initialized to 10.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the totalPages state variable. This will track the total number of pages available for pagination.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've correctly declared both 'totalPages' and 'setTotalPages' using useState, and initialized it to 10.
steps.feedbackWrong: The totalPages state wasn't properly initialized. Make sure to use useState with an initial value of 10, and declare both the variable and setter function.

steps.title: Define handlePrevious function
steps.instruction: Inside your Pagination component, define a function named handlePrevious that decrements the currentPage state by 1, but prevents it from going below 1.
steps.hint: Create a function that uses setCurrentPage with the previous state value. Use a condition to check if the current page is greater than 1 before decrementing.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handlePrevious function is defined that safely decreases the current page number.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the handlePrevious function that safely decrements the page number.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function properly prevents the page number from going below 1.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handlePrevious function isn't defined correctly. Remember to use setCurrentPage and ensure the page doesn't go below 1.

steps.title: Define handleNext function
steps.instruction: Define a function named handleNext that increments the currentPage state by 1, but ensures it doesn't exceed totalPages.
steps.hint: Create a function that uses setCurrentPage to update the state. You can use the current state value to calculate the next page.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleNext function that increments currentPage by 1, but doesn't go beyond totalPages.
successCriteria: The handleNext function should be defined inside the component, use setCurrentPage, and ensure the new page doesn't exceed totalPages.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the handleNext function. This function will allow users to navigate to the next page while respecting the total page limit.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a function, but it might not properly handle the page increment or the totalPages limit. Make sure to use setCurrentPage and ensure the new value doesn't exceed totalPages.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleNext function is not defined correctly. You need to create a function that increments currentPage by 1 while ensuring it doesn't go above totalPages.

steps.title: Return a container div from the component
steps.instruction: Inside the Pagination component, return a div element from the component's return statement.
steps.hint: Replace the existing empty div with a proper div element that will contain your pagination UI.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a div element that will serve as the container for the pagination UI.
successCriteria: The component returns a JSX div element in its return statement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've returned a container div from the Pagination component. This provides the structure we'll use to build the pagination UI.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're returning a div element from the component's return statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should return a div element. Check that you're returning JSX from the component.

steps.title: Add a Previous button inside the container
steps.instruction: Inside the container div, add a button element with the text 'Previous'.
steps.hint: Add a <button> tag with 'Previous' as its content. Place it inside the existing <div>.
steps.analogousExample: // Example of adding a button inside a container div>
steps.expectedOutcome: The container div now contains a button with the text 'Previous'.
successCriteria: The button element with text 'Previous' is present inside the container div.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the Previous button to the pagination UI.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added a button with the exact text 'Previous' inside the container div.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Previous button is missing or not correctly placed inside the container div.

steps.title: Wire the Previous button's onClick to handlePrevious
steps.instruction: Add an onClick handler to the Previous button that calls the handlePrevious function when clicked.
steps.hint: Use the onClick prop on the button element and pass handlePrevious as the handler.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of wiring a button click to a handler
<button onClick={handlePrevious}>Previous</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The Previous button will respond to clicks and call the handlePrevious function.
successCriteria: The button element has an onClick prop
The onClick prop's value is handlePrevious
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully wired the Previous button to call the handlePrevious function when clicked.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the onClick handler isn't quite correct. Make sure you're passing handlePrevious directly to the onClick prop.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Previous button doesn't have the correct onClick handler. Remember to add onClick={handlePrevious} to the button element.

steps.title: Display current page information
steps.instruction: Add a <span> element inside the container div that displays the current page and total pages in the format 'Page {currentPage} of {totalPages}'.
steps.hint: Use JSX interpolation with curly braces to insert the state values into the text.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show the current page number and total pages in a text format.
successCriteria: Use JSX interpolation with curly braces
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a span that displays the current page information. The state values are now visible in the UI.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your span displays both currentPage and totalPages in the exact format 'Page {currentPage} of {totalPages}' using JSX interpolation.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try adding a <span> element that shows the current page and total pages. Use the format 'Page {currentPage} of {totalPages}' with the state variables inside curly braces.

steps.title: Add a Next button inside the container
steps.instruction: Add a button element with the text 'Next' inside the container div, after the current page display.
steps.hint: Add a <button>Next</button> element in the return statement, after the span that shows the page information.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will now have a 'Next' button in the UI, placed after the page information.
successCriteria: Button placed after the page display span
Button is inside the container div
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the Next button to complete the navigation controls.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added a button with the exact text 'Next' and placed it after the page display.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Next button is missing or incorrectly placed. Add a <button>Next</button> element after the page display span.

steps.title: Wire the Next button's onClick to handleNext
steps.instruction: Add an onClick handler to the Next button that calls the handleNext function. The Next button is already present in your code.
steps.hint: Add the onClick attribute to the Next button and set it to call handleNext.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of wiring a button click to a handler
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The Next button will now respond to clicks and call the handleNext function to increment the current page.
successCriteria: The Next button has an onClick attribute
The onClick attribute calls the handleNext function
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully wired the Next button to call the handleNext function. Now both navigation buttons are fully functional.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added the onClick attribute to the Next button and set it to call handleNext.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Next button still needs an onClick handler. Add onClick={handleNext} to the Next button.
